analysis.one_liner: Would have shut down the labor board's enforcement of workers' union rights until its disputed appointments were resolved.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate labor committee after referral in April 2013; it drew 16 cosponsors, all Republicans, and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In January 2012, the president appointed three members to the National Labor Relations Board while the Senate was in recess, and opponents argued those appointments were invalid. This bill would have responded by ordering the board to stop all business that requires a quorum, and to stop enforcing or carrying out any board decision, rule, or vote issued since January 4, 2012. In practice, that would have frozen enforcement of the nation's private-sector union and labor law until the disputed members were confirmed by the Senate or the Supreme Court ruled on the appointments. The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers with pending disputes before the National Labor Relations Board, and businesses resisting union organizing campaigns or board rules, would have benefited. Every board decision, rule, and vote issued since January 4, 2012 could no longer be implemented, administered, or enforced, and the board itself would have halted all quorum-requiring activity until the impasse over its membership was resolved [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required the board to cease all activity requiring a quorum and barred it from appointing personnel or implementing, administering, or enforcing any decision, rule, vote, or other action taken since January 4, 2012 [S2][S3].

Those prohibitions would have stayed in place until either a full quorum of board members was confirmed by the Senate, the Supreme Court ruled on the constitutionality of the January 2012 appointments, or the first session of the 113th Congress ended [S3].

The board is the enforcement agency for private-sector labor law, so freezing it removes the forum where workers file unfair labor practice complaints and where union elections and organizing disputes are decided [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who rely on the board to enforce their rights to organize, bargain collectively, and challenge retaliation would have borne the cost: their pending complaints could not be decided, and rulings already won since January 4, 2012 could not be enforced [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Shutting down board activity would have left both sides in labor disputes without a forum: workers' complaints would sit unresolved, and employers would face the same ambiguity the bill's own title describes, with two years of board rulings in limbo [S2][S3].

The bill would not have merely blocked new decisions; it would have retroactively unenforced actions already finalized, so unions and workers who won rulings between January 2012 and enactment could lose them pending re-consideration by a confirmed board [S3].

Because labor law covers the full range of disputes, a frozen board also removes a check on union misconduct and on employers alike, trading short-term relief for some employers against months of unresolved cases across the economy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a targeted benefit to employers contesting board actions but at the price of suspending the government's labor-law enforcement machinery entirely, retroactively as well as prospectively. The cost would fall on any worker or employer with a live dispute, and the mechanism — freezing the whole board rather than litigating the appointments case — addressed a constitutional dispute by disabling the agency at the center of it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2013, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat with no further action until the Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Lamar Alexander introduced the bill on April 25, 2013, with 16 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the action history before the 113th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No board actions were voided, so workers and unions kept the board as their enforcement forum; the employers the bill was written for gained nothing from it.

for.name: Lamar Alexander
for.role: U.S. Senator from Tennessee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to halt National Labor Relations Board activity and enforcement of board actions dating to January 2012 [S1][S3].

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Republican (16 of 16), and the bill never advanced past referral in a Senate where the committee chairman's party held the majority, so no vote was ever scheduled [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers contesting union organizing or board rulings
industries.note: The bill would have voided enforcement of every board decision, rule, and vote issued since January 4, 2012, letting those employers escape rulings already issued against them. Workers' ability to organize and contest unfair labor practices would weaken accordingly [S3].

Unions depend on the board to certify elections, rule on unfair labor practices, and enforce bargaining obligations; a board halted and stripped of two years of decisions removes the main forum protecting their members' rights [S2][S3].
